title: The Church That Outlived Rome
subtitle: Rome fell and the church did not. Slaves, monks, queens, and grieving scholars carried the faith to the peoples who broke the empire, and by the year 1000 Europe was baptized. What kind of victory that was is the harder question.

sections.title: The City Falls and the Church Does Not
sections.body:
In August of 410 a Gothic army under Alaric entered Rome and sacked it for three days. As sacks go it was restrained, since the Goths were themselves Christians of a sort, Arians who spared the churches and those sheltering in them. It did not matter. Rome had not fallen to an enemy in eight hundred years, and the shock ran to the edges of the world. In Bethlehem the old scholar Jerome wrote that his voice stuck in his throat, that the city which had taken the whole world had itself been taken. Pagans said the old gods were avenging their abandoned altars, and the charge stung enough that Augustine spent thirteen years writing the City of God to answer it. In 476 the last western emperor, a boy, was quietly deposed, and no one bothered to appoint another. The order that had governed the Mediterranean for half a thousand years was gone.

Here is the fact this essay exists to weigh. The church did not go down with the ship. The institution most entangled with the empire proved to be the one thing that crossed the wreck intact, and more than intact. In the five centuries after Rome fell, the faith converted the very peoples who had broken it, until the map of Europe was a map of the baptized. How that happened is one of the great stories the church has to tell. Whether it was entirely a victory is a question the story itself will force.

sections.title: Patrick and the Edge of the World
sections.body:
The new mission age began at the empire's broken edge, with a kidnapping. Patrick was a Roman Briton, the teenage son of a churchman's family, when Irish raiders took him in a slave raid and sold him to herd animals on cold hills. He was about sixteen. In six years of slavery the family faith he had ignored became his own, prayer upon prayer in the sleet, and after an escape and a return home he did the thing that still astonishes. He went back. Sometime in the middle of the fifth century Patrick returned to the people who had enslaved him, this time carrying the gospel, and he spent the rest of his life among them. We know this because he wrote it down himself, in a rough Latin Confession that opens by calling himself a sinner and the least of the faithful. It is one of the oldest surviving documents from any victim of the slave trade, and it forgives.

Ireland had never been Roman. This was the faith's first great leap beyond the old imperial fence, and the leap kept going. Irish monasteries became mission stations. In 563 Columba crossed to the island of Iona to work among the Picts, and around 590 Columbanus crossed to the continent and planted monasteries through Gaul and into Italy, and from Iona, Aidan came south in 635 to evangelize Northumbria from Lindisfarne. Within a century the converted had become the converters. That pattern, the gospel rebounding from its newest edge, is the engine of this whole era.

sections.title: Clovis, the Sword, and the Problem of Numbers
sections.body:
On the continent the conversions came differently, from the top. Around 496, the traditional date, Clovis, the brutal and brilliant king of the Franks, was baptized, and the chronicler Gregory of Tours says three thousand of his warriors followed him into the water. His wife Clotilda, a Christian princess, had worked on him for years, and a battlefield bargain finished the work, victory in exchange for allegiance to her God. It reads uncomfortably like a treaty. In 597 the pattern repeated in Kent, where King Ethelbert, married to a Christian Frankish queen, received a band of Roman missionaries and eventually the font, and his people followed by the thousand.

Be honest about what such baptisms were. When a king converts and his war band files into the river behind him, we are not looking at three thousand Damascus roads. We are looking at loyalty, politics, and the ancient assumption that a people shares its lord's gods. Historians argue about how deep it went, and both sides of the argument hold real evidence. Paganism persisted under the surface for generations, in charms and offerings and hedged bets, and church councils complained about it for centuries. And yet the wells slowly filled. Through parishes, penance, monasteries, and mothers, the descendants of the baptized war bands began producing saints, scholars, and reformers no one could call nominal. Both things are true. The conversion of Europe was shallow, and it deepened. Any telling that keeps only one half is propaganda for somebody.

sections.title: Gregory, the Monks, and the Long Patience
sections.body:
Behind the Kentish mission stood the most consequential bishop of the age. Gregory the Great, a Roman aristocrat who had turned his family house into a monastery, was dragged unwillingly into the papacy in 590, governed a starving city the empire had effectively abandoned, fed it from church lands, and still found the will to look outward. Bede tells the story, perhaps polished by time, that Gregory had once seen fair-haired English boys for sale in a Roman market and said they were not Angles but angels, and the idea of a mission to their island never let him go. In 597 he sent Augustine, a reluctant monk who tried to turn back once, with a company of brothers to Kent.

Gregory's instructions, preserved by Bede, are a small classic of missionary wisdom. Do not demolish the people's temples, he wrote to the mission, only the idols inside them. Cleanse the buildings and set altars in them, and let the festival days be redirected to better ends, for a stubborn people climbs to God by steps and not by leaps. One can hear in that letter both a deep pastoral patience and the seed of every later compromise, the old gods lingering inside the new calendar, and honesty keeps both readings. The mission took root. Within two generations the English church was producing scholars of its own, and within a century it was exporting missionaries back to the continent, most famously Boniface, who felled the Germans' sacred oak at Geismar, spent decades organizing their church, and died at pagan hands in 754, an old man, holding up a gospel book, the story says, as the swords came down.

sections.title: Alphabets, Envoys, and the Millennium
sections.body:
The eastern half of the story has its own texture, and its gift was written language. In 863 two brothers from Thessalonica, Cyril and Methodius, scholars fluent in Slavonic, went north to Moravia at a prince's request and did what the western missions rarely did. They built the converts an alphabet. They translated the Scriptures and the liturgy into the people's own tongue, and when Frankish clergy objected that God could properly be worshiped only in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, Cyril answered, his early Life records, that the rain of God falls on all alike. The brothers were harried over that objection all their lives, and after their deaths their disciples were expelled from Moravia. Bulgaria took the refugees in, and from their school came the alphabet that bears Cyril's name and still carries the worship and literature of much of the Slavic world.

The drama moved at last to Kyiv. In 988 Vladimir, prince of the Rus, weighing the faiths of his neighbors, chose the Christianity of Constantinople, and the old chronicle preserves the report of his envoys, who had stood in the great church of Hagia Sophia and no longer knew whether they were on earth or in heaven. The story is polished, and the politics under it were real, a marriage alliance and an emperor's need for soldiers. It was also the beginning of a thousand years of Slavic Christianity in the east. Meanwhile the north came in, kingdom by kingdom, Denmark in the 960s, then Norway, until around the year 1000 the assembly of Iceland, pressed to choose one law for one people, chose baptism.

sections.title: What Kind of Victory
sections.body:
Now the hard accounting, because this era carries the church's shame as well as its glory, and sometimes in the same event. The gospel that crossed to Ireland in a freed slave's forgiveness also crossed the Elbe at the point of Charlemagne's sword. His wars against the pagan Saxons ran for three decades, his own royal annals record a day at Verden in 782 when thousands of Saxon prisoners were beheaded, and his law code made refusing baptism a capital crime. The court scholar Alcuin protested in letters that faith comes from the will and cannot be compelled, that a man can be dragged to the font but not to belief. He was right, he said it at the time, and he was ignored. We do not get to place that history outside the family. The hands that forced the Saxons were baptized hands.

So what kind of victory was the conversion of Europe? An honest ledger reads like this. The faith outlived the empire that had adopted it, which suggests its life never came from empire. It traveled best with its least armed carriers, slaves and monks and queens and grieving old scholars, and worst wherever it rode with power, a pattern the church had every chance to learn and largely refused. By the year 1000 Europe was baptized, and Europe was not converted, and the medieval church would live inside that difference for centuries. So does every church since, including ours. Baptism can be administered. Conversion must still be preached, person by person, and no king can order it. That is the lesson of five hundred years. We are slow students.

keyFigures.name: Patrick
keyFigures.note: Enslaved as a boy by Irish raiders, he returned to Ireland with the gospel in the middle of the fifth century.

keyFigures.name: Gregory the Great
keyFigures.note: The monk made pope in 590 who fed Rome and sent the mission to the English.

keyFigures.name: Augustine of Canterbury
keyFigures.note: Reluctant leader of the Kentish mission of 597, first archbishop of Canterbury.

keyFigures.name: Columba
keyFigures.note: Irish abbot who crossed to Iona in 563 and worked among the Picts.

keyFigures.name: Boniface
keyFigures.note: English missionary who felled the Germans' sacred oak, organized their church, and was killed in 754.

keyFigures.name: Alcuin of York
keyFigures.note: Charlemagne's scholar, who protested that faith cannot be forced, and was ignored.

keyFigures.name: Cyril and Methodius
keyFigures.note: Brothers from Thessalonica who gave the Slavs an alphabet and worship in their own tongue.

keyFigures.name: Vladimir of Kyiv
keyFigures.note: Prince whose baptism in 988 brought the Rus into the church of Constantinople.
